newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgians celebrate national day, scars on show.
newsitem.headline: Belgians celebrate national day, scars on show.

text.p: Belgians celebrated their national day in a blazing sun on Monday after a painful year that included a child sex and murder scandal and a large-scale political corruption affair.
The scars were still in evidence as Belgians responded to a plea from King Albert to regain morale and fight on.
Thousands looked on as over 3,000 members of the military, police and fire civil protection sector mounted the traditional parade in front of the Royal Palace.
A paratroop battalion at the centre of accusations of maltreating Somali children during a humanitarian mission in 1993 got a hostile reception at the parade.
Photographers and Belgian radio said small sections of the crowd whistled and booed along the route as the Third Paratroops Battalion marched past.

Reuters photographers said that mingling in the crowd and handing out white flags, balloons and photos of murdered children were 1,000 white-clad people from groupings set up around the country to keep up pressure for a full investigation into why four children died at the hands of a paedophile ring.
"We want to celebrate national day...but insist that things have to change in the Belgian state. We want to go right up to the end," one of them told Belgian television.

Ahead of National Day on Sunday King Albert told his people that no stone should be left unturned in finding out whether the culprits in the paedophilia scandal exposed last summer got high-level protection.

There have been growing allegations of protection for Marc Dutroux, who is alleged to have murdered four children and imprisoned and sexually abused two others, and fears that the commission will be prevented from getting at the truth.

A quarter of a million people took to the streets last October for a "white march" in support of the parents of the scandal and in protest at what they see as a corrupt and morally bankrupt justice system.

Two members of the Third Paratroops Battalion who have since left the unit were cleared by a Belgian military court last month of maltreating a Somali child during a mission to the African country in 1993 because of insufficient evidence.
A number of intellectuals had made calls in the media for the battalion to stay away from the parade as a symbolic act of sorrow at the incident.

Belgian Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet rejected the calls on Belgian television on Sunday, saying any wrong acts had been carried out by individuals and that nothing had been found wrong in the battalion as a whole.
